title: Harvard Gains $12 Million To Link Quantum Computing With Artificial Intelligence
excerpt: Harvard gains $12 million to link quantum computing with artificial intelligence, led by Mikhail Lukin.
content:
A $12 million federal grant will fund a Harvard-led collaboration aiming to link quantum computing with artificial intelligence. The project, Application-Aware Error Correction Codesign for Scientific Quantum Computing (ASQC), is part of the Department of Energy’s Genesis Mission and unites researchers from MIT, Cornell University and three national labs alongside tech partners NVIDIA and Anthropic.

Mikhail Lukin, Harvard’s Joshua and Beth Friedman University Professor and co-founder of QuEra Computing, will lead the effort. University President Alan M. Garber added, “Mikhail is a visionary leader. He will do an excellent job both driving progress and strengthening partnerships to ensure America’s competitiveness in this area of vital importance.”

AI Accelerates Quantum Error Correction for Scientific Computing

Recent advances in quantum error correction (QEC) have enabled the suppression of errors to the point where adding qubits now reduces, rather than increases, computational errors; a critical step toward building larger, more complex quantum computers. This progress is being further accelerated by a Harvard-led collaboration that has secured $12 million from the U.S. Department of Energy to develop an artificial intelligence-driven, fault-tolerant QEC system.

The team has already demonstrated the power of AI in improving QEC performance; a neural-network decoder, described in an April preprint, reduced error rates by up to 17 times and operated thousands of times faster than existing software. This decoder identifies errors during computation, which is essential for maintaining the integrity of quantum calculations. Alongside these academic institutions, technology partners NVIDIA and Anthropic are contributing their expertise.

This broad partnership reflects the complexity of the task and the need for diverse skillsets. “This kind of collaborative approach is really needed in this case. We want to make something that no one else has been able to make,” Lukin stated.

The team intends to test the AI-designed error correction codes on hardware at Harvard, MIT and QuEra Computing, where Lukin also serves as co-founder and chief scientist. The ultimate goal, according to Lukin, is to unlock solutions to previously intractable scientific problems.

“I think as we build larger and better quantum computers, we will really start making more and more scientific discoveries,” he said, envisioning a future where quantum computers act as powerful new tools for exploration, “you can really explore corners of the universe where you have never been, like a new kind of telescope.” The team believes that these advances will bring long-held dreams of the quantum computing community within reach, stating, “We can really see these dreams the community has had for the last 40 years, for the first time, in the direct line of sight.”

Genesis Mission Unites Institutions to Advance Quantum-AI Collaboration

The collaborative effort extends beyond traditional academic boundaries, with the Department of Energy grant specifically encouraging partnerships between universities and national laboratories. Lukin explained that this approach is unusual in quantum computing research, where institutions often operate more independently, and is essential to achieving goals previously considered unattainable. The project builds upon prior work addressing the inherent instability of qubits, the fundamental building blocks of quantum computers, and seeks to mitigate the impact of environmental noise.

Lukin views the resulting quantum computer not merely as a faster calculator, but as a novel scientific instrument capable of exploring previously inaccessible realms of knowledge. This expanded potential is fueled by advances in artificial intelligence, which Lukin believes will dramatically accelerate progress.
